questions.question: In much of the world, summer, autumn, winter and spring follow one another in the same order every year. What causes the seasons?
choices: The tilt of Earth's axis
Earth's distance from the Sun
The Sun's heat rising and falling
The Moon's pull on Earth
questions.context: Earth's axis is tilted, so as Earth travels around the Sun, each half of Earth takes its turn leaning toward the Sun and then away from it. Earth's distance from the Sun changes by only about 5 million kilometres out of some 150 million, far too little to make summer and winter. The Sun's own output barely changes, and the Moon's pull raises the tides, not the seasons.
questions.grade_note: That the tilt of Earth's axis, not its distance from the Sun, causes the seasons is the core of the 6th-grade seasons unit (TEKS 6.9A, NGSS MS-ESS1-1).

questions.question: Earth's path around the Sun is not a perfect circle but a very slightly stretched oval, so its distance from the Sun changes a little through the year. When is Earth closest to the Sun?
choices: In early January
In early July
In late March
In late September
questions.context: Earth comes closest to the Sun around January 3, at about 147 million kilometres, and is farthest in early July, at about 152 million. The Northern Hemisphere has its winter while Earth is nearest the Sun, which shows that distance does not make the seasons.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade seasons lessons teach that Earth is nearest the Sun in early January, the plainest evidence against the distance explanation.

questions.question: Snow falls across Canada in late December, as winter sets in over the Northern Hemisphere. What season is beginning in the Southern Hemisphere at the same time?
choices: Summer
Winter
Spring
Autumn
questions.context: The two hemispheres always have opposite seasons. In late December the Southern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun and gets the more direct light and the longer days, so in Australia, Christmas comes in early summer, a day for barbecues and the beach.
questions.grade_note: Opposite seasons in the two hemispheres follow directly from the tilt and are a standard 6th-grade seasons fact.

questions.question: Earth spins on a tilted axis, and it carries that axis along on its year-long trip around the Sun. As Earth travels around, what happens to the direction its axis points in space?
questions.answer: It keeps pointing the same way all year
choices: It keeps pointing the same way all year
It turns to keep leaning toward the Sun
It rocks back and forth through the year
It stands straight up in spring and autumn
questions.context: The axis stays pointed the same way in space, its northern end aimed almost at Polaris, the North Star, all year. So on one side of the orbit the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and six months later, on the far side, it leans away. In spring and autumn the axis is still tilted; it simply leans neither toward the Sun nor away from it.
questions.grade_note: The axis keeping one direction in space as Earth orbits is the step the 6th-grade seasons model is built on (TEKS 6.9A: model how the tilted Earth revolves around the Sun).

questions.question: The Sun stands high over a town in Canada at noon in June. At noon in December, it hangs low in the sky, and its light strikes the ground at a slant. Why does the low December Sun warm the town less than the high June Sun does?
questions.answer: Its energy is spread over more ground
choices: Its energy is spread over more ground
The town is farther from the Sun then
The Sun itself gives off less energy then
Earth spins faster in the winter months
questions.context: A slanting beam spreads the same sunlight over a wider patch of ground, so each patch gets less, the way a flashlight tilted to a slant makes a bigger, dimmer spot. The town is not farther from the Sun in December, the Sun's output hardly changes, and Earth spins at the same steady rate all year.
questions.grade_note: Direct against slanting sunlight, with the energy of a low Sun spread over more area, is the 6th-grade reason summer is warmer than winter.

questions.question: The Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun in late June. That week, a traveller sets off from the equator and heads north toward the North Pole. What happens to the hours of daylight as she goes?
questions.answer: They grow longer, up to 24 hours
choices: They grow longer, up to 24 hours
They grow shorter, down to none
They stay about 12 hours all the way
They grow longer, then shorter again
questions.context: With the North Pole tipped toward the Sun, more of each day's spin keeps the far north in sunlight, so the days lengthen the farther north the traveller goes. North of the Arctic Circle the Sun does not set at all in late June, the midnight sun, while at the equator the day stays close to 12 hours all year.
questions.grade_note: Longer days in the hemisphere leaning toward the Sun are part of the 6th-grade seasons line; the lengthening toward the pole is its plainest consequence.

questions.question: Thousands of people gather at Stonehenge, in England, to watch the Sun rise on the June solstice, around June 21. What makes that day special in the Northern Hemisphere?
questions.answer: It has the most daylight of the year
choices: It has the most daylight of the year
It has the least daylight of the year
Its day and night are equal in length
Earth comes nearest to the Sun that day
questions.context: On the June solstice the Northern Hemisphere leans most toward the Sun and has its longest day, while the Southern Hemisphere has its shortest. Stonehenge's main axis points to the sunrise on that day. The word solstice comes from Latin words for the Sun standing still.
questions.grade_note: The solstices as the longest and shortest days of the year are named in the 6th-grade seasons line.

questions.question: Spring begins in the Northern Hemisphere around March 20, and autumn in the Southern. Around September 22, it is the other way round. How do day and night compare across Earth on those two dates?
choices: They are about equal everywhere
Days are longer in the Northern Hemisphere
Days are longer in the Southern Hemisphere
Nights are longer than days everywhere
questions.context: These are the equinoxes, from Latin words for equal night. Earth's axis then leans neither toward the Sun nor away from it, so the noon Sun is overhead at the equator and day and night last about 12 hours each all over Earth. Day is in fact slightly longer, because the air bends sunlight and the Sun is a disc, not a point.
questions.grade_note: The equinoxes, when day and night are about equal everywhere, are named in the 6th-grade seasons line.

questions.question: Suppose Earth's axis stood straight up, with no tilt at all, as Earth travelled around the Sun on its usual path. What would happen to the seasons?
choices: They would almost disappear
They would stay just as they are
They would grow much stronger
They would each last twice as long
questions.context: With no tilt, each place would get the same slant of sunlight and the same length of day all year, so summer and winter would almost vanish. Only Earth's small change in distance from the Sun would warm and cool it a little. A bigger tilt makes the seasons stronger, and a smaller one makes them milder.
questions.grade_note: Reasoning that no tilt means almost no seasons checks the 6th-grade idea that the tilt, not distance, makes them.

questions.question: Earth's spinning axis does not stand straight up from the flat plane of its path around the Sun. It leans, and classroom globes copy that lean on their stands. About how far does Earth's axis lean from straight up?
choices: About 23.5 degrees
About 66.5 degrees
About 45 degrees
About 10 degrees
questions.context: Earth's axis leans about 23.5 degrees from straight up. Measured from the flat plane of the orbit instead, it stands at about 66.5 degrees, so the two numbers always add up to 90. Over some 41,000 years the lean slowly shifts between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees.
questions.grade_note: The size of Earth's tilt, about 23.5 degrees, is stated in the 6th-grade seasons line and shown on every classroom globe.
